modules.title: Database Design and Normalization
modules.goal: Model entities and relationships so the schema stays correct as it grows.

topics.title: Data Modeling Basics
topics.simple: Schema design entities, attributes aur relationships se shuru hota hai.
topics.pro: Data modeling identifies the nouns, their attributes and the relationships before tables are written.

example.sql: -- students, courses and enrollments are the core entities

topics.title: Entities
topics.simple: Entity ek real-world object ya concept hai.
topics.pro: An entity becomes a table, with each row representing one instance of that concept.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Attributes
topics.simple: Attributes entity ke properties hote hain.
topics.pro: Attributes become columns with a type, nullability and constraints that reflect the domain.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT UNIQUE, marks INTEGER CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100));

topics.title: Keys
topics.simple: Keys rows ko identify aur relate karte hain.
topics.pro: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key references another table’s key and enforces the relationship.
points: Primary key is unique and not null.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Relationships
topics.simple: Relationships cardinality batate hain.
topics.pro: Relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; the cardinality determines where keys live.
points: 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: One-to-One
topics.simple: 1:1 relationship me har row ka ek partner hota hai.
topics.pro: A one-to-one relationship uses a unique foreign key or a shared primary key, often to split optional or sensitive data.
points: Sharing the primary key is common.
Do not use it for unrelated data.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE student_profiles (student_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES students(id), bio TEXT);

topics.title: One-to-Many
topics.simple: 1:N relationship me parent ke multiple children hote hain.
topics.pro: The foreign key lives on the many side, pointing back to the one parent.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Many-to-Many
topics.simple: M:N relationship ke liye junction table chahiye.
topics.pro: A junction table stores one row per pair and can carry relationship attributes such as enrollment date.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Normalization
topics.simple: Normalization duplication aur update anomalies kam karta hai.
topics.pro: Normalization organizes data into related tables so each fact is stored once and updated in one place.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: First Normal Form
topics.simple: 1NF atomic values aur repeating groups hataata hai.
topics.pro: First normal form requires atomic column values and no repeating groups or arrays masquerading as columns.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: Second Normal Form
topics.simple: 2NF partial dependencies hataata hai.
topics.pro: Second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, grade TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Third Normal Form
topics.simple: 3NF transitive dependencies hataata hai.
topics.pro: Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);

topics.title: BCNF
topics.simple: BCNF strong normal form hai.
topics.pro: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_rooms (course_id INTEGER, room TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (course_id, room));

topics.title: Denormalization
topics.simple: Denormalization performance ke liye duplication add karta hai.
topics.pro: Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE courses ADD COLUMN enrolled_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

topics.title: Surrogate vs Natural Keys
topics.simple: Surrogate key generated hota hai; natural key business value hai.
topics.pro: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact.
points: Keep a unique natural key when needed.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE);

topics.title: Junction Tables
topics.simple: Junction table M:N relationship ko rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: A junction table has foreign keys to both sides and usually a composite primary key over the pair.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id BIGINT REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Audit Columns
topics.simple: Audit columns created/updated timestamps rakhte hain.
topics.pro: created_at and updated_at columns make data changes observable and support debugging and reporting.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();

topics.title: Soft Deletes
topics.simple: Soft delete row ko flag karta hai, remove nahi.
topics.pro: A deleted_at timestamp hides rows without physically removing them, but every query must filter it.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ;

topics.title: Schema Naming
topics.simple: Clear names schema ko understandable banate hain.
topics.pro: Consistent table, column and constraint names reduce mistakes and make migrations predictable.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE course_enrollments (student_id BIGINT, course_id INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));

topics.title: Practical School Schema
topics.simple: Students, courses aur enrollments ka clean schema banao.
topics.pro: A school schema uses students and courses as entities and enrollments as the many-to-many junction with its own attributes.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Data Modeling Basics in a production query.
interview.answer: Data modeling identifies the nouns, their attributes and the relationships before tables are written. Key rules: Find entities. List attributes. Define relationships.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Entities in a production query.
interview.answer: An entity becomes a table, with each row representing one instance of that concept. Key rules: Students are an entity. Courses are an entity. Enrollments connect them.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Attributes in a production query.
interview.answer: Attributes become columns with a type, nullability and constraints that reflect the domain. Key rules: Choose precise types. Mark required attributes. Avoid overloaded columns.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key references another table’s key and enforces the relationship. Key rules: Primary key is unique and not null. Foreign keys enforce relationships. Keys should be stable.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Relationships in a production query.
interview.answer: Relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; the cardinality determines where keys live. Key rules: 1:1 shares a key. 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side. M:N needs a junction table.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain One-to-One in a production query.
interview.answer: A one-to-one relationship uses a unique foreign key or a shared primary key, often to split optional or sensitive data. Key rules: Use a unique foreign key. Sharing the primary key is common. Do not use it for unrelated data.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain One-to-Many in a production query.
interview.answer: The foreign key lives on the many side, pointing back to the one parent. Key rules: Parent key is referenced. Child holds the foreign key. Index the foreign key.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Many-to-Many in a production query.
interview.answer: A junction table stores one row per pair and can carry relationship attributes such as enrollment date. Key rules: Two foreign keys. Composite primary key. Relationship attributes live here.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Normalization in a production query.
interview.answer: Normalization organizes data into related tables so each fact is stored once and updated in one place. Key rules: Reduce duplication. Avoid update anomalies. Normalize first, denormalize deliberately.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain First Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: First normal form requires atomic column values and no repeating groups or arrays masquerading as columns. Key rules: One value per cell. No repeating columns. Give each row a key.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Second Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: Second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key. Key rules: Start with 1NF. Check composite keys. Move partial dependencies out.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Third Normal Form in a production query.
interview.answer: Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes. Key rules: Start with 2NF. Move derived facts out. Keep each fact once.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain BCNF in a production query.
interview.answer: Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys. Key rules: Stronger than 3NF. Check all determinants. Split overlapping keys.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Denormalization in a production query.
interview.answer: Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity. Key rules: Measure first. Document the duplication. Keep it synchronized.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Surrogate vs Natural Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact. Key rules: Surrogates are stable. Natural keys can change. Keep a unique natural key when needed.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Junction Tables in a production query.
interview.answer: A junction table has foreign keys to both sides and usually a composite primary key over the pair. Key rules: One row per relationship. Add relationship attributes. Index both foreign keys.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Audit Columns in a production query.
interview.answer: created_at and updated_at columns make data changes observable and support debugging and reporting. Key rules: Default created_at to now. Update updated_at deliberately. Store timestamps with time zone.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Soft Deletes in a production query.
interview.answer: A deleted_at timestamp hides rows without physically removing them, but every query must filter it. Key rules: Add deleted_at. Filter in queries or views. Hard-delete when policy requires.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Schema Naming in a production query.
interview.answer: Consistent table, column and constraint names reduce mistakes and make migrations predictable. Key rules: Use snake_case. Plural table names are common. Name keys and constraints explicitly.

interview.q: Module 21 · Explain Practical School Schema in a production query.
interview.answer: A school schema uses students and courses as entities and enrollments as the many-to-many junction with its own attributes. Key rules: Keys first. Foreign keys next. Constraints last. Index relationship columns.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Data Modeling Basics matter?
logic.answer: Data modeling identifies the nouns, their attributes and the relationships before tables are written. Find entities. List attributes. Define relationships.
An entity becomes a table, with each row representing one instance of that concept. Students are an entity. Courses are an entity. Enrollments connect them.
Attributes become columns with a type, nullability and constraints that reflect the domain. Choose precise types. Mark required attributes. Avoid overloaded columns.

A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key references another table’s key and enforces the relationship. Primary key is unique and not null. Foreign keys enforce relationships. Keys should be stable.
Relationships are one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; the cardinality determines where keys live. 1:1 shares a key. 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side. M:N needs a junction table.

A one-to-one relationship uses a unique foreign key or a shared primary key, often to split optional or sensitive data. Use a unique foreign key. Sharing the primary key is common. Do not use it for unrelated data.
The foreign key lives on the many side, pointing back to the one parent. Parent key is referenced. Child holds the foreign key. Index the foreign key.
A junction table stores one row per pair and can carry relationship attributes such as enrollment date. Two foreign keys. Composite primary key. Relationship attributes live here.
Normalization organizes data into related tables so each fact is stored once and updated in one place. Reduce duplication. Avoid update anomalies. Normalize first, denormalize deliberately.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does First Normal Form matter?
logic.answer: First normal form requires atomic column values and no repeating groups or arrays masquerading as columns. One value per cell. No repeating columns. Give each row a key.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Second Normal Form matter?
logic.answer: Second normal form removes attributes that depend on only part of a composite key. Start with 1NF. Check composite keys. Move partial dependencies out.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Third Normal Form matter?
logic.answer: Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes. Start with 2NF. Move derived facts out. Keep each fact once.
Boyce-Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing remaining anomalies from overlapping keys. Stronger than 3NF. Check all determinants. Split overlapping keys.
Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data to speed reads, accepting extra write complexity. Measure first. Document the duplication. Keep it synchronized.

logic.q: Module 21 · Why does Surrogate vs Natural Keys matter?
logic.answer: A surrogate key is a generated identifier, while a natural key comes from the domain; surrogate keys are stable and compact. Surrogates are stable. Natural keys can change. Keep a unique natural key when needed.
